title: The Micro Threshold
use_cases: Use when evaluating the first 250 words of a manuscript for narrative hooks
Implement when establishing worldbuilding through character action rather than exposition
Configure when defining the emotional resonance between a protagonist and their stakes
Use when auditing a story'ating voice to ensure it reflects a survival mindset or specific character traits
content:
Sitting at Prim’s knees, guarding her, is the world’s ugliest cat. Mashed-in nose, half of one ear missing, eyes the color of rotting squash. Prim named him Buttercup, insisting that his muddy yellow coat matched the bright flower. He hates me. Or at least distrusts me. Even though it was years ago, I think he still remembers how I tried to drown him in a bucket when Prim brought him home. Scrawny kitten, belly swollen with worms, crawling with fleas. The last thing I needed was another mouth to feed. But Prim begged so hard, cried even, I had to let him stay. It turned out okay. My mother got rid of the vermin and he’s a born mouser. Even catches the occasional rat. Sometimes, when I clean a kill, I feed Buttercup the entrails. He has stopped hissing at me.

In 270 words, Collins also sets up promise, voice, and tone, but in a different way.

Here the narrator and character voice are one and the same. It’s practical and competent. It reveals a love of family without being sentimental, and demonstrates a survival mindset. Katniss is also straightforward, not beating around the bush or asking for sympathy when talking about drowning the cat to save food.

The tone has a quality of restrained tenderness, layered over some obvious economic hardship. This is underscored by dread: something bad this way comes.

And that brings us to the promise, which is less clearly stated the Pride & Prejudice but still completely shown to the reader.

“This is the day of the reaping” is like a ticking clock in this story. Reaping could mean a harvest of crops, but based on the focus on hunger and survival, and Prim’s bad dreams, we can assume it’s not. It’s something sinister, and it’s happening soon.

The information we know by the end of the micro-threshold tells us everything. Katniss loves Prim. She wants to protect her, and Prim is innocent and vulnerable. Whatever the reaping is, it’s almost sure to threaten their relationship. We know resources are scarce and morality is shaped by hunger, implying hard choices are normal for Katniss. And because her voice is competent and self-aware, Collins is telling us we are in the hands of a capable protagonist who will act when the threat appears.

Our expectations of this story are set.

Also, note how well the worldbuilding is handled in this brief passage. No exposition dumps. No history lesson taking up valuable real-estate. We start with Katniss, in her ordinary life (that we know is about to change or be threatened), but details like the shared bedroom, the mother’s beaten-down nature, and cleaning a kill give us a sense of the character’s situation without over-explaining.

Your job as the writer is to not just begin the story, but set up the voice, tone, and promise of what’s to come.

Both of these excerpts start with ordinary life, but also with something that will obviously push the characters out of the ordinary in short order.

As an exercise, try copying your first 250ish words into a blank document and read it in isolation, looking specifically for those markers.
